scenes.tts: Why would potassium flow into a cell, against a 28-fold concentration difference? Take a cell with 140 millimolar potassium inside and 5 outside. Hold it at minus 70 millivolts and open potassium channels. Potassium leaves. Hold it at minus 100, and potassium comes in.
scenes.caption: Why would potassium flow into a cell, against a 28-fold concentration difference? Take a cell with 140 mM K+ inside and 5 mM outside. Hold it at −70 mV and open potassium channels. Potassium leaves. Hold it at −100 mV, and potassium comes in.
scenes.visual: THE WORLD FOR THE WHOLE FILM: a thick horizontal membrane band across the middle of the frame (about 1/5 of frame height), OUTSIDE above (pale blue fluid, label 'OUTSIDE 5 mM K+'), INSIDE below (warm tan fluid, label 'INSIDE 140 mM K+'). K+ ions are small orange dots labelled 'K+' once; many dots below, few above, all jittering slowly the whole film. One potassium channel is a gap in the band with two rounded gate blocks. On the right edge, a vertical voltage ruler labelled 'Vm' from 0 at top to -120 mV at bottom, with a teal pointer. Opening frame: the cell picture with a large '?' over the channel and a '28x' badge on the crowded side. On 'minus 70 millivolts' the teal pointer slides down to -70 and the gate blocks swing open; on 'Potassium leaves' dots stream up through the channel. On 'minus 100' the pointer slides to -100, the stream slows, stops and reverses: dots now stream down into the cell. The '28x' badge pulses on 'comes in'.
scenes.narration: Why would potassium flow into a cell, against a 28-fold concentration difference? Take a cell with 140 mM K+ inside and 5 mM outside. Hold it at −70 mV and open potassium channels. Potassium leaves. Hold it at −100 mV, and potassium comes in.

scenes.visual: Title card 'Two Pushes, One Hill' over the same cell picture, which keeps jittering; dots now stream in slowly. At most 2 seconds.

scenes.tts: An ion feels two pushes. The first is concentration: potassium drifts from where it is crowded to where it is scarce. The second is voltage. The membrane potential is the inside minus the outside, and a negative inside pulls positive ions in.
scenes.caption: An ion feels two pushes. The first is concentration: potassium drifts from where it is crowded to where it is scarce. The second is voltage. The membrane potential, Vm, is the inside minus the outside, and a negative inside pulls positive ions in.
scenes.visual: Zoom so the channel and the band fill most of the frame height; the ruler stays at right. Just before 'concentration', the crowd of dots below pulses and a thick orange arrow grows upward (outward) through the channel; label it 'concentration push' when named. During 'The second is', a row of minus signs fades in along the inner face of the band and plus signs along the outer face; a thick teal arrow grows downward (inward), then gains the label 'voltage push' when named. On 'pulls positive ions in' a few dots near the channel drift toward the minus signs. Dots keep jittering throughout.
scenes.narration: An ion feels two pushes. The first is concentration: potassium drifts from where it is crowded to where it is scarce. The second is voltage. The membrane potential, Vm, is the inside minus the outside, and a negative inside pulls positive ions in.

scenes.tts: Add the two pushes into one number. Picture the trip into the cell as a hill with two slopes. The concentration slope makes entering uphill. The voltage slope makes it downhill. Net flow always goes the way the total runs downhill.
scenes.visual: The two arrows lift off the channel and become two ramp segments in an inset to the left of the channel, titled 'energy to enter (schematic)': an orange segment rising from OUTSIDE to INSIDE (labelled 'concentration slope') and a teal segment falling (labelled 'voltage slope'). On 'the total' the two segments merge into one white ramp whose tilt is their sum; a small orange ball sits on it and rolls the way the ramp tilts. Keep the teal pointer at -70 for now, so the white ramp tilts uphill-to-enter and the ball rolls slowly toward OUTSIDE while the narrator finishes.
scenes.narration: Add the two pushes into one number. Picture the trip into the cell as a hill with two slopes. The concentration slope makes entering uphill. The voltage slope makes it downhill. Net flow always goes the way the total runs downhill.

scenes.tts: For each ion, one voltage makes the two slopes cancel. That is its equilibrium potential. For potassium, with these teaching values at body temperature, the Nernst equation puts it at minus 89.1 millivolts. There, ions still cross, but equal numbers go each way.
scenes.caption: For each ion, one voltage makes the two slopes cancel. That is its equilibrium potential. For potassium, with these teaching values at 37 °C, the Nernst equation puts E_K at −89.1 mV. There, ions still cross, but equal numbers go each way.
scenes.visual: The teal pointer slides slowly down the ruler; as it moves, the teal ramp segment steepens and the white ramp flattens. On 'cancel' the white ramp is level and the ball stops. A green tick and label 'E_K = -89.1 mV' appear on the ruler at that point. On 'equal numbers go each way' dots cross independently and randomly up and down. Separate counters tick at different instants and settle at '12 out • 12 in' over this schematic interval, with 'net 0' below. Ruler marks are exact; the ramp heights are computed from the lesson's two-push values (concentration +8.59 kJ/mol; voltage -6.75 kJ/mol at -70 mV, -9.65 at -100 mV).
scenes.narration: For each ion, one voltage makes the two slopes cancel. That is its equilibrium potential. For potassium, with these teaching values at 37 °C, the Nernst equation puts E_K at −89.1 mV. There, ions still cross, but equal numbers go each way.

scenes.tts: So compare the voltage with that green mark. At minus 70 millivolts, which way does potassium go? And at minus 100? Decide before the picture moves.
scenes.caption: So compare the voltage with that green mark. At −70 mV, which way does potassium go? And at −100 mV? Decide before the picture moves.
scenes.visual: Ruler fills the right third: green E_K mark at -89.1, and two hollow teal markers at -70 and -100, each with a '?' beside it. The channel and white ramp reset to neutral (ramp level, no stream). Question card at top: 'Which way at each voltage?' The '?' marks pulse gently; dots jitter.
scenes.narration: So compare the voltage with that green mark. At −70 mV, which way does potassium go? And at −100 mV? Decide before the picture moves.

scenes.visual: Hold the question card and both '?' markers on screen. Only the ambient jitter of the dots and a slow pulse of the '?' marks move. Near-silence.

scenes.tts: Minus 70 sits above the green mark. The voltage slope is shallower than the concentration slope, so entering is uphill, and potassium leaves. Minus 100 sits below it. Entering is downhill, so potassium comes in.
scenes.caption: −70 mV sits above the green mark. The voltage slope is shallower than the concentration slope, so entering is uphill, and potassium leaves. −100 mV sits below it. Entering is downhill, so potassium comes in.
scenes.visual: Question card fades. On 'Minus 70' the teal pointer jumps to -70 (above the green mark); the teal ramp segment shrinks shorter than the orange one, the white ramp tilts uphill-to-enter, the ball rolls toward OUTSIDE and dots stream up out of the channel; a label 'uphill to enter: K+ out'. On 'Minus 100' everything resets in one move (stream stops, label clears, ramp level), then the pointer slides to -100 (below the mark), the teal segment grows longer than the orange, the white ramp tilts downhill-to-enter, the ball rolls toward INSIDE and dots stream down into the cell; label 'downhill to enter: K+ in'.
scenes.narration: −70 mV sits above the green mark. The voltage slope is shallower than the concentration slope, so entering is uphill, and potassium leaves. −100 mV sits below it. Entering is downhill, so potassium comes in.

scenes.tts: That is the rule for passive flow. Find the equilibrium potential and compare the voltage with it. For a positive ion, a voltage above the mark sends net flow out. Below the mark, net flow goes in. For a negative ion, the rule flips.
scenes.caption: That is the rule for passive flow. Find the equilibrium potential, then compare Vm with it. For a positive ion, Vm above the mark sends net flow out. Below the mark, net flow goes in. For a negative ion, the rule flips.
scenes.visual: The numbered potassium ruler morphs into an unnumbered generic comparison bar filling the frame's right half, with the channel at left and a green mark labelled 'E_X (this ion)'. On 'above the mark' the region above the ion's own E_X tints faintly orange with an upward arrow 'net out'; on 'Below the mark' the region below tints teal with a downward arrow 'net in'. On 'negative ion' the 'K+' chip changes to a generic 'X−' chip; the mark now explicitly means that anion's own E_X, and the two arrows swap direction with a half-turn.
scenes.narration: That is the rule for passive flow. Find the equilibrium potential, then compare Vm with it. For a positive ion, Vm above the mark sends net flow out. Below the mark, net flow goes in. For a negative ion, the rule flips.

scenes.tts: The channel did the same thing in both cases. It opened a path, and it chose which ion could use it, and how fast. The slopes chose the direction. Channels and passive carriers never decide which way.
scenes.visual: The chip returns to 'K+'. Split the channel picture into two copies side by side, left at -70 (dots streaming out) and right at -100 (dots streaming in); both channel shapes are identical and both glow on 'the same thing'. On 'which ion' one sodium dot (grey, labelled 'Na+') bounces off the channel mouth. On 'The slopes chose the direction' the two small white ramps appear over each copy, tilted opposite ways. Streams keep flowing.
scenes.narration: The channel did the same thing in both cases. It opened a path, and it chose which ion could use it, and how fast. The slopes chose the direction. Channels and passive carriers never decide which way.

scenes.tts: How does a cell move anything uphill? It couples that trip to one running further downhill. The sodium pump splits ATP to push three sodium out and bring two potassium in. Then SGLT1 lets two sodium run downhill into the cell, and that run pays for glucose to climb.
scenes.caption: How does a cell move anything uphill? It couples that trip to one running further downhill. The sodium pump splits ATP to push 3 Na+ out and bring 2 K+ in. Then SGLT1 lets 2 Na+ run downhill into the cell, and that run pays for glucose to climb.
scenes.visual: Back to one membrane band filling the frame. Left: a block labelled 'Na+/K+ pump' with an 'ATP' chip entering and cracking in two, relabelled 'ATP split', on 'splits ATP'; three grey 'Na+' dots go up and out, two orange 'K+' dots come down and in, on the words. Right: a block labelled 'SGLT1'. On 'two sodium run downhill' two Na+ dots slide down a steep teal ramp into the cell through SGLT1; on 'glucose to climb' a rounded yellow chip labelled 'glucose' is carried up a shorter yellow ramp alongside them (schematic heights). The pump never touches the glucose chip.
scenes.narration: How does a cell move anything uphill? It couples that trip to one running further downhill. The sodium pump splits ATP to push 3 Na+ out and bring 2 K+ in. Then SGLT1 lets 2 Na+ run downhill into the cell, and that run pays for glucose to climb.

scenes.tts: Every crossing follows the same hill. A channel or passive carrier only opens the way. Add up the slopes of everything that moves together, and the total must run downhill.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the opening cell picture with the channel, the pump and SGLT1 all in the band. Over each, a small white ramp shows its total: channel ramp at -100 mV tilting downhill-to-enter, pump ramp (ATP plus ions) tilting down, SGLT1 ramp (sodium plus glucose) tilting down. Mark the three-ramp comparison 'schematic'. On 'the total must run downhill' all three balls roll down their ramps at once.
scenes.narration: Every crossing follows the same hill. A channel or passive carrier only opens the way. Add up the slopes of everything that moves together, and the total must run downhill.

scenes.visual: End card: 'The total must run downhill.' over the softly jittering cell picture.
